title: Theory of Computation
description: Build a rigorous understanding of formal languages, automata, computability, reductions, and complexity classes, while developing the proof habits needed to reason about the limits of computation.

topics.title: Mathematical Logic and Proof for Computation
topics.description: Theory of computation is proof-driven. This opening unit makes students fluent in the symbolic language, proof patterns, and formal precision needed for the rest of the course.

children.title: Propositional and predicate logic
children.description: Students learn how formal statements are built, interpreted, negated, and used as the raw material of specifications and machine models.

children.title: Proof techniques
children.description: The goal is to make claims about infinite sets of strings, machines, and languages feel manageable through reusable proof patterns.

children.title: Sets, relations, and functions
children.description: These structures give precise vocabulary for languages, transitions, encodings, reductions, and simulations.

topics.title: Alphabets, Strings, Languages, and Formal Models
topics.description: Before studying machines, students need a shared model of what machines read, produce, and recognize. This unit turns computation into a mathematical object.

children.title: Strings and languages
children.description: Students learn to treat collections of strings as decision problems, which is the central abstraction of the course.

children.title: Decision problems and recognizers
children.description: This frames computation as yes/no classification, making later comparisons between automata, Turing machines, and complexity classes clean.

children.title: Modeling assumptions
children.description: Students see why simple abstract machines can reveal general truths about all computing devices.

topics.title: Finite Automata
topics.description: Finite automata are the first machine model: limited memory, precise behavior, and enough power to model lexical patterns, protocols, and simple controllers.

children.title: Deterministic finite automata
children.description: DFAs show how computation can be represented as state evolution over an input string.

children.title: Nondeterministic finite automata
children.description: NFAs introduce branching as a modeling convenience and prepare students for later nondeterministic complexity.

children.title: Automata design and invariants
children.description: Students learn to prove that a machine recognizes exactly the intended language, not merely to draw state diagrams.

topics.title: Regular Languages and Expressions
topics.description: This unit connects machine recognition to algebraic descriptions of patterns, making regularity both operational and syntactic.

children.title: Regular expressions
children.description: Regular expressions provide a compact language-building notation and connect theory to practical pattern matching.

children.title: Closure properties
children.description: Closure gives a toolkit for building new regular languages from known ones while preserving recognizability.

children.title: Equivalence of representations
children.description: Students learn that DFAs, NFAs, and regular expressions describe exactly the same class of languages.

topics.title: Nonregularity and Lower Bounds for Finite Memory
topics.description: Not every pattern can be recognized with finite memory. This unit teaches students how to prove impossibility, a central habit of theoretical CS.

children.title: Pumping lemma for regular languages
children.description: The pumping lemma gives a reusable contradiction method for showing that finite automata cannot remember enough.

children.title: Myhill-Nerode theorem
children.description: Myhill-Nerode reveals regularity through distinguishable prefixes and gives a sharper view of minimal memory.

children.title: Finite-memory lower bounds
children.description: Students learn to translate intuitive memory limitations into formal state-count arguments.

topics.title: Context-Free Grammars and Languages
topics.description: Context-free grammars model recursive structure, such as nested parentheses and programming-language syntax, which finite automata cannot handle.

children.title: Grammar definitions and derivations
children.description: Students learn how recursive production rules generate languages and parse structural patterns.

children.title: Grammar design
children.description: The point is to move from informal recursive descriptions to exact grammars that generate all and only desired strings.

children.title: Normal forms
children.description: Normal forms standardize grammars so they can be analyzed and converted algorithmically.

topics.title: Pushdown Automata and Parsing Connections
topics.description: Pushdown automata add a stack to finite control. This gives the first concrete model of unbounded but disciplined memory.

children.title: PDA mechanics
children.description: Students see how stacks make nested and recursive language recognition possible.

children.title: Acceptance by final state or empty stack
Equivalence with CFGs
children.description: The equivalence between PDAs and CFGs ties generative syntax to operational recognition.

children.title: Parsing and syntax applications
children.description: This bridges theory to compilers and programming languages without turning the course into implementation.

topics.title: Non-Context-Free Languages
topics.description: This unit extends impossibility proof skills to recursive structures and shows the limits of a single stack.

children.title: Pumping lemma for CFLs
children.description: Students learn how to prove that some languages require more coordination than context-free grammars provide.

children.title: Ogden's lemma and stronger tools
children.description: World-class coverage should expose students to sharper methods even if not every proof is assigned in depth.

children.title: Closure and decision properties
children.description: Students learn which operations and questions remain tractable for context-free languages.

topics.title: Turing Machines and Equivalent Models
topics.description: Turing machines are the course's general model of computation. They let students reason about what is computable independent of any particular hardware or language.

children.title: Turing machine definitions
children.description: Students learn the formal parts of a machine powerful enough to capture general algorithms.

children.title: Variants and robustness
children.description: Different machine variants all compute the same class of functions, which supports the Church-Turing thesis.

children.title: Encoding machines and inputs
children.description: Self-reference and undecidability require treating machines themselves as data.

topics.title: Decidability, Recognizability, and the Halting Problem
topics.description: This unit establishes the boundary between problems solvable by algorithms and problems that no algorithm can decide.

children.title: Decidable and recognizable languages
children.description: Students distinguish guaranteed termination from partial recognition, a subtle but essential theoretical divide.

children.title: The halting problem
children.description: The halting problem is the canonical impossibility result and the gateway to diagonalization.

children.title: Classic undecidable problems
children.description: Students learn to recognize undecidability patterns across machine behavior and formal systems.

topics.title: Reducibility and Undecidability Proofs
topics.description: Reductions are the language of comparison: they show that solving one problem would solve another known-hard problem.

children.title: Mapping reductions
children.description: Students learn a disciplined proof template for transferring undecidability from one language to another.

children.title: Turing reductions
children.description: Oracle-style reductions broaden the idea of solving one problem using another as a subroutine.

children.title: Proof design patterns
children.description: The point is to make reductions feel like engineering a logical trap: any solver for the target would break a known impossibility.

topics.title: Time Complexity and Efficient Computation
topics.description: After computability asks what can be solved at all, complexity asks what can be solved with feasible resources.

children.title: Asymptotic time on machine models
children.description: Students learn to measure algorithms in a model-independent way while respecting simulation costs.

children.title: Class P
children.description: P formalizes efficient deterministic computation and becomes the baseline for tractability.

children.title: Examples from graph and arithmetic problems
Time hierarchy
children.description: Hierarchy theorems show that more time really can buy more computational power.

topics.title: Nondeterminism, NP, and NP-Completeness
topics.description: NP-completeness is the course's major bridge to algorithms, optimization, cryptography, and practical intractability.

children.title: Class NP
children.description: Students learn NP as efficiently verifiable search, not just as nondeterministic guessing.

children.title: Polynomial-time reductions
children.description: These reductions compare the difficulty of efficient computation while preserving yes/no answers.

children.title: Canonical complete problems
children.description: Students learn how SAT anchors NP-completeness and how reductions propagate hardness across domains.

topics.title: Space Complexity and Hierarchy Theorems
topics.description: Space complexity reveals that memory can be a more subtle resource than time and introduces classes central to modern theory.

children.title: Space-bounded computation
children.description: Students model machines with restricted work tape and see how memory limits shape solvability.

children.title: PSPACE and complete problems
children.description: PSPACE captures problems solvable with polynomial memory, often involving games, logic, and quantified formulas.

children.title: Hierarchy results
children.description: Hierarchy theorems give formal evidence that resource classes do not collapse trivially.

topics.title: Randomized, Counting, and Advanced Complexity
topics.description: A world-class theory course should show how randomness, counting, interaction, and approximation reshape the landscape beyond P and NP.

children.title: Randomized computation
children.description: Students learn how algorithms can use random choices and how complexity classes track allowable error.

children.title: Counting complexity
children.description: Counting versions of decision problems expose a different kind of hardness.

children.title: Interactive and probabilistically checkable proofs
children.description: This gives students a window into modern complexity without requiring a full second course.

topics.title: Theory in Modern CS: Algorithms, Languages, Cryptography, and Verification
topics.description: The final unit connects formal theory to the broader CS curriculum so students see computation theory as a living toolkit, not a sealed-off subject.

children.title: Algorithmic hardness and approximation
children.description: Students learn how theory explains why some optimization problems resist exact efficient algorithms.

children.title: Programming languages and semantics
children.description: Automata, grammars, lambda calculus, and decidability all reappear in language design and formal semantics.

children.title: Cryptography and verification
children.description: Complexity assumptions and formal models support secure protocols and software correctness.
